summary: Two players each command a deck representing their squads, playing cards to move, spot, suppress, or attack across a hex battlefield inspired by real WWII skirmishes in North Africa. As units take casualties their cards leave the deck (or go into a wound pile), so your options visibly degrade over the course of a scenario, mirroring the attrition of the fight.
praised: elegant fusion of deckbuilding with a tactical wargame
quick to teach despite deep tactics
criticised: card draw luck can swing a scenario
later campaign missions can feel unbalanced
deck thinning can snowball for the player already ahead

interaction.kind: direct combat and line-of-fire on a shared hex map
interaction.detail: Units from both sides occupy the same hex map and directly shoot, suppress, and eliminate each other's cards from play, permanently weakening the opponent's deck. Almost the entire game state — the map, unit positions, and casualties — is shared and contested every turn, with no meaningful private board.
interaction.said: reviewers call it a tight two-player tactical duel — 'a chess-like battle', 'brutal card and casualty management', combat that directly whittles the other side's deck

subsystems: objective/VP-token control on the map (scenario-specific victory conditions)
sources: VP tokens earned each round for controlling objective hexes
scenario-specific bonus objectives (e.g. eliminating key units, exiting units off-board)
scoring.how_you_win: Play command cards to activate and move/attack with your units, holding more objective hexes than your opponent to rack up VP faster and hit the scenario's VP threshold first (or fulfill the mission's special win condition) before your deck is worn down by casualties.

theme.said: praised as an elegant simulation where deck-building itself IS the tactical attrition — reviewers note it avoids "pasted-on" complaints because casualties physically leave your deck
theme.why: wounded/killed units are removed from your card pool rather than just losing hit points, so your deck literally shrinks and weakens as your unit takes real losses, modeling attrition rather than abstracting it.

style.why: A tight deck/bag-building economy and card-driven action selection carry the game, with combat and dice present but casualties attritional rather than eliminating, keeping it hybrid rather than full wargame.
